hazards.blocked-spill-kit-decoy: Those boxes are stacked right across the spill kit station. The one time this kit actually matters is the one time nobody can afford to dig it out from behind a pallet — it stays clear, always.
hazards.dirty-cart-return-decoy: That cart came straight off a soiled run and it's parked in the clean bay. A soiled cart in the clean bay contaminates every clean linen load that touches that space next, which defeats the entire reason the two bays are kept apart.
hazards.mixed-waste-stream-decoy: That yellow hazardous-drug container has ordinary food wrapper and general trash sitting in it. Mixing anything into a dedicated stream doesn't just contaminate that bin — it turns everything else in it into the same problem the label was written to contain.
hazards.unprotected-sharps-handling-decoy: There's a sharp visibly poking through that bag, and a bare-handed squeeze is exactly what's about to happen to it. A bag that shows a sharp through the plastic gets set down and handled with the tool built for it, never compressed or squeezed by hand to make it fit.

interrupts.alert: A bag turns up on the sorting line with no colour coding and no label at all — it could be general or it could be regulated.
interrupts.missNote: The unlabeled bag went into general waste on a guess. If it was actually regulated, every bag it touched on the way there now has the same question hanging over it.
interrupts.why: An unlabeled bag is treated as the more hazardous stream until someone with the authority to say otherwise actually looks at it — guessing it into general waste because it's probably fine is exactly the shortcut that turns this room's whole segregation system into a coin flip.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the call to the supervisor — an unlabeled bag doesn't get sorted on a guess.

interrupts.alert: While you're still finishing the first cleanup, a second spill is spotted a few feet away.
interrupts.cue: One kit, one spill at a time — this one needs another set of hands.
interrupts.missNote: Both spills got worked at once, alone. Neither one actually got the kit's full, uninterrupted process, which is the only way either one counts as contained.
interrupts.why: Splitting attention between two active spills is how both end up half-contained instead of one being handled properly — the second spill gets cordoned and backup called, not started solo while the first one is still open.
interrupts.wrongNote: Call for backup — a second spill doesn't get folded into whatever you're already doing.

lateNotes.log-pickup: Hold that. The hauler hasn't actually taken the load yet.
lateNotes.seal-manifest-container: Not yet — the container has to be weighed first, or the manifest is recording a number nobody actually checked.
lateNotes.sealed-container: Nothing sealed and manifested yet — there's nothing ready to move to the dock.

name: Linen & Regulated Waste Handling

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Gown, gloves and eye protection before the first bag comes off the chute.
steps.prompt: Gown, gloves and eye protection before the first bag comes off the chute.
steps.title: Don PPE for the waste room
steps.why: Everything that reaches this room is contaminated until proven otherwise — OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard treats this job the same as any other exposure risk, because a soiled bag doesn't announce what's actually inside it.

steps.cue: Pull each bag off the chute landing and stage it for inspection before it moves any further.
steps.prompt: Pull each bag off the chute landing and stage it for inspection before it moves any further.
steps.title: Receive bags from the chute
steps.why: The chute is where every floor's laundry lands in one place, from a routine room change to whatever a code or a fall left behind — staging it here rather than carrying it straight through to the sorters is what gives this room its one real chance to catch a problem bag before it ever reaches the line.

steps.cue: Two bags on this landing have a problem that gets worse the further they travel. Find them.

itemNames.leaking-bag: a bag leaking through the plastic
itemNames.overweight-bag: a bag packed past its weight limit

itemNotes.leaking-bag: Fluid working through the plastic here means it's already on whatever this bag has touched since it left the floor — it gets contained now, not carried the rest of the way to the sorter first.
itemNotes.overweight-bag: A bag packed well past its weight limit is a strain injury waiting for whoever lifts it next — it gets split into two bags at the correct weight, not muscled onto the scale as one.

steps.prompt: Two bags on this landing have a problem that gets worse the further they travel. Find them.
steps.title: Inspect every bag before it moves on
steps.why: A bag looks the same whether it's fine or failing until somebody actually checks it — this inspection is what catches a leak or an overweight bag while it's still sitting still on the landing, rather than partway down the sorting line where a leak has already spread and an overweight bag has already been lifted.

steps.cue: Contain the leaking bag inside a second bag before it goes anywhere else.
steps.prompt: Contain the leaking bag inside a second bag before it goes anywhere else.
steps.title: Double-bag the leaking bag
steps.why: A second bag around a leaking one is what stops the contamination at this landing instead of on the cart, the floor, or the next person's gloves — it is the whole reason double-bagging exists as a step rather than a suggestion.

steps.cue: Place today's waste into the regulated, general and sharps containers, each in its own bin.
steps.prompt: Place today's waste into the regulated, general and sharps containers, each in its own bin.
steps.title: Sort into the three separate streams
steps.why: General, regulated and sharps waste are hauled, treated and disposed of under completely different rules — a stream that gets mixed at the sorting stage stays mixed all the way to disposal, which turns a bin of ordinary trash into a bin of regulated medical waste that now has to be treated as one.

steps.cue: Read the scale and confirm the container is within its rated weight before you seal it.

gauge.label: CONTAINER WEIGHT
gauge.missNote: Sealed a container you never actually confirmed was within its rated weight. Reopen it and check before it goes any further.

steps.prompt: Read the scale and confirm the container is within its rated weight before you seal it.
steps.title: Weigh the regulated container before sealing
steps.why: Every regulated waste container has a weight rating set by its own manufacturer — a container sealed over that limit is a container that can split, buckle or fail exactly where a hauler has to lift and stack it, and a failure at that point spreads whatever the container was holding across a dock full of other people's loads.

steps.cue: Seal the lid and fill in the manifest tag before the container leaves this room.
steps.prompt: Seal the lid and fill in the manifest tag before the container leaves this room.
steps.title: Seal the container and complete the manifest
steps.why: The manifest is what makes this container's contents, weight and origin something the hauler and the facility can both be held to later — a container that leaves without one is untraceable the moment it's out the door, and untraceable is exactly the state regulated waste is never supposed to reach.

steps.cue: Two containers on this dock aren't ready to go out. Find them.

itemNames.mislabeled-container: a container with no biohazard label
itemNames.overfilled-bin: a bin packed past its fill line

itemNotes.mislabeled-container: A regulated waste container with no biohazard label on it reads as ordinary trash to everyone downstream who never opens it to check — the label goes on before it ever reaches the dock, not after someone asks where it went.
itemNotes.overfilled-bin: A bin forced shut past its fill line is one more item away from splitting the next time someone tries to close it — it gets emptied into a fresh container, not pressed down to make room.

steps.prompt: Two containers on this dock aren't ready to go out. Find them.
steps.title: Scan the staging area before loading
steps.why: The dock is the last place anything gets caught before it becomes the hauler's problem instead of this room's — a scan here, right before loading, is what keeps a labelling gap or an overfilled bin from riding out the door unnoticed and turning into someone else's discovery later.

steps.cue: Apply the spill kit's absorbent and hold the containment steady through the full cleanup.
steps.holdBreakNote: The cleanup broke off before the spill was fully contained. A spill treated halfway is still a spill anyone can walk through.
steps.prompt: Apply the spill kit's absorbent and hold the containment steady through the full cleanup.
steps.title: Respond to the spill with its kit
steps.why: A body-fluid spill kit is built to be used start to finish in one motion — absorbent down, contained, disposed of as regulated waste — and stopping partway through leaves exactly the kind of half-contained spill the kit exists to prevent.

steps.cue: Roll the sealed, manifested container to its marked slot on the loading dock.

drag.missNote: Not in the marked slot — a container left off to the side is easy for the hauler to miss on pickup.

steps.prompt: Roll the sealed, manifested container to its marked slot on the loading dock.
steps.title: Move the sealed container to the dock
steps.why: The dock slot is where the hauler expects to find exactly what the manifest describes, in the order the pickup route runs — a container parked anywhere else, even a few feet away, is a container the pickup can miss entirely and this room has to explain going nowhere on the manifest that says it left.

steps.cue: Turn the wash valve and run the empty linen cart through its full cycle.
steps.prompt: Turn the wash valve and run the empty linen cart through its full cycle.
steps.title: Run the cart washer
steps.why: An empty cart still carries whatever it was hauling right up until it's actually washed, not just emptied out — running it through the washer before it goes anywhere near the clean bay is what keeps yesterday's soiled load off today's clean linen instead of just out of sight.

steps.cue: Confirm the washed cart is fully dry before releasing it to the clean bay.
steps.prompt: Confirm the washed cart is fully dry before releasing it to the clean bay.
steps.title: Release the cart once it's dry
steps.why: A cart released wet carries moisture into a clean linen load the same way a soiled one carries contamination — dry and actually confirmed is the real bar for clean here, not just recently run through the washer and pushed straight back into service.

steps.cue: Unload today's delivery and shelve it on the clean linen rack.

itemNames.shelve-stock: shelve it on the clean rack

steps.prompt: Unload today's delivery and shelve it on the clean linen rack.
steps.title: Restock the clean linen supply
steps.why: A floor that runs out of clean linen mid-shift reaches for whatever's closest, which is exactly how corners get cut elsewhere in the building — keeping this shelf actually stocked, unloaded and shelved rather than left sitting on a pallet by the door, is what keeps that pressure from building up in the first place.

steps.cue: Record the hauler's pickup and today's container count in the log.
steps.prompt: Record the hauler's pickup and today's container count in the log.
steps.title: Log the pickup and the shift's count
steps.why: The log is what lets this facility answer, months later, exactly how much regulated waste left the building on a given day and who signed it out — a shift that isn't logged is a shift regulators and auditors alike have no record of.
